title: Operational fallback messaging: outage scenarios and sales hooks
body:
TL;DR: This note frames a targeted GTM messaging brief for platform and ops buyers focused on real-world failure modes of managed hyperscaler endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure) and succinct sales hooks for Redwood. Rather than generic "cost vs latency" talking points, this doc prioritizes outage/fallback scenarios, runbooks, and concrete buyer-safe assurances (SLOs, predictable fallbacks, auditability).

Audience and persona focus:
- Primary: Platform engineering / infra teams evaluating managed endpoints for customer-facing products (SRE, infra platform, ML infra).
- Secondary: Security/compliance and engineering managers who need continuity and deterministic behavior for egress-sensitive or regulated apps.

Common hyperscaler managed-endpoint failure patterns we've observed (and sales implications):
1) Regional capacity exhaustion during traffic spikes
   - What happens: sudden throttling or delayed queueing; opaque autoscaling causes request variance and retries.
   - Hyperscaler behavior: auto-scale can be slow or capped by account limits; customer sees variable tail-latency and opaque throttling reasons.
   - Sales hook: Redwood offers capacity tiers + predictable reserved pools and can pre-warm/route across regions with transparent capacity signals.
2) Model/variant downgrades and silent quality regressions
   - What happens: managed provider swaps to a cheaper variant or temporary fallback model without clear audit trail.
   - Hyperscaler behavior: internal fallback choices are not always surfaced to customers; post-mortem is slow.
   - Sales hook: Redwood exposes model variant metadata, rollout controls, and immediate observable fallbacks with alerts and rollback policies.
3) Network egress bottlenecks and multi-region failover gaps
   - What happens: cross-region requests spike egress costs or encounter ACLs/NAT exhaustion; failovers are manual or incomplete.
   - Hyperscaler behavior: managed endpoints often assume cloud-native egress, leaving customers to solve networking.
   - Sales hook: Redwood Private + Dedicated allow VPC-aware routing, pre-configured multi-region policies, and deterministic egress budgeting guidance.
4) Billing spikes from retry storms or cold-cache token bursts
   - What happens: one incident multiplies tokens and causes unpredictable invoice surges.
   - Hyperscaler behavior: per-request metering + opaque caching behavior leads to surprise charges.
   - Sales hook: Redwood Optimize and token-level tracing makes root-cause of token spikes explorable and billable units attributable to routes/teams.
5) Compliance blackout / air-gapped maintenance windows
   - What happens: vendor maintenance or region-level incidents trigger data residency or audit risks.
   - Hyperscaler behavior: patching and maintenance schedules may not align with regulated windows.
   - Sales hook: Redwood Private gives a separation between control plane and data plane, scheduled maintenance SLAs, and on-prem options for windows when regulators require absolute isolation.

How hyperscalers typically respond (patterns to call out in sales conversations):
- Opacity: Limited telemetry surfaced to customer, encouraging trial-and-error debugging.
- One-size-fits-all autoscaling: fast on paper but unpredictable under tail loads.
- Centralized fallback policies: default fallbacks that prioritize platform resilience over customer fidelity.
- Billing-first throttles: cost-control mechanisms that impact availability without transparent negotiation.

Top-level value propositions and buyer promises (short lines for use in email threads and pitch decks):
- "Predictable inference economics — no surprise invoices when traffic or token patterns spike."
- "Deterministic fallbacks — we surface and control model swaps so you never lose SLAs silently."
- "Regional-aware routing and reserved capacity for critical paths — multi-region != guesswork."
- "Auditable rollout and fallback events for compliance and post-incident analysis."

Example sales scripts (ops-first hooks):
- Opening: "Many teams we work with initially picked hyperscaler managed endpoints for speed-to-market — and later got burned by noisy autoscaling and billing surprises. Can I walk you through a few real outage patterns and how customers use reserved capacity + model rollouts to avoid them?"
- Objection ("We have native autoscaling, why change?"): "Autoscaling is great for average load but many of our customers needed the ability to pin capacity for peak journeys and visibility into why fallbacks happen — autoscale doesn't give you token-level visibility or rollout controls."
- Objection ("Hyperscalers are cheaper at scale"): "Hyperscalers can be economical when everything behaves; what we sell is reduced out-of-band operational cost — fewer incident hours, fewer postmortem escalations, and predictable unit economics for your customer-facing features."

Technical rebuttals / talking points for solution engineers:
- Telemetry: demo token-level cost traces and a sample incident where a retry storm was traced to a misconfigured circuit-breaker.
- Rollouts: show a canary -> A/B -> force-fallback policy with immediate rollback inside the Console.
- Network: present a VPC routing diagram showing Dedicated worker pools and controlled egress to customer's NAT/GW.
- SLA: show example latency percentiles under reserved capacity vs open managed endpoints during a simulated spike.

Suggested collateral & assets to attach to outreach:
- Short one-pager: "Failure modes we see in managed endpoints — and how to avoid them" (2 pages).
- Runbook template for incident responders: quick checks and telemetry queries to identify model fallback vs network vs quota.
- Mini-demo script: simulate quota/region saturation and demonstrate Redwood fallback and rollback in < 5 minutes.

Sales enablement checklist (what to arm AEs/SEs with):
- One-slide summary of "How we behave during a region outage" (what customer sees, what Redwood does).
- Replayable demo with synthetic workload and toggles for reserved capacity.
- Pricing example showing "surge protection" via reserved vs on-demand capacity.
- Two scripts: 1) initial discovery question set for ops concerns, 2) incident-driven renewal/re-sell script.

Open product asks (to hand to product/engineering):
- Expose clearer event logs for "fallback cause" (variant, capacity, policy) as a first-class time-series. Owner: @Miguel R. (JIRA: INF-2330).
- Add a "surge-protection" policy toggle to automatically switch to pre-paid reserved capacity when tail-latency crosses threshold (configurable). Owner: @Asha K.
- Build a demo harness to replay regional saturation across clouds (GCP/AWS/Azure) so sales can show consistent behavior. Owner: Solutions eng.

Next steps / owners:
- GTM draft for external one-pager: Claire to produce v0 by 2024-09-25.
- SE demo harness plan: Miguel to draft infra notes and resource estimate by 2024-10-02 (JIRA-GTM-1427).
- Product sync: triage feature asks in next PM weekly on 2024-10-06.

Appendix: short competitor notes (ops lens)
- AWS-managed endpoint style: strong integration with other AWS services, but default autoscaling + regional-first defaults can hide fallback logic. Often requires account-level quota increases to prevent capacity failures.
- GCP-managed endpoint style: developer ergonomics are good; however, multi-region egress and private peering are more manual to configure, leading to network surprises in cross-region failovers.
- Azure-managed endpoint style: enterprise integrations and identity story are strong; default fallbacks and cost-control mechanisms are sometimes tied to subscription policies, making incident remediation reliant on billing/ownership conversations.

Notes to self / risks:
- Avoid promising 100% elimination of incidents; focus on reducing MTTI/MTTR and predictable economics.
- Watch legal language around SLAs vs Reserved capacity — coordinate with Legal for compliant claim language.
